rationale: A wins because it keeps the story sellable without dressing unknowns as facts: "Wise says stablecoin rails are cheaper — the open question is who keeps the savings" turns the missing margin detail into the actual question. B has useful shapes, but "The stablecoin boring-infrastructure moment" and "the end of 'crypto or settlement'" are cleverer than they are proven. Both sets know the unnamed stablecoin and partner are the weak spot; A handles that weakness with more discipline.
gaps_in_A: "Stablecoins get a mainstream payments test" is valid, but it still leans on the broad adoption frame; it needs a named comparable or analyst proof before it can claim stablecoin settlement is "crossing into regulated, mainstream B2B money movement."
The correspondent-banking angle says "which bank fees and float revenue get squeezed"; the update supports faster/cheaper settlement, but not float economics specifically.
A asks for a named customer only in questions/refusals; it could have made clearer that without one, all four kept angles remain announcement-led rather than adoption-led.
gaps_in_B: "£30B stablecoin bet" overstates the fact pattern. Wise moves £30B per quarter overall; the update does not say that volume is moving through stablecoin settlement or that Wise is betting that amount.
"EU MiCA, U.S. stablecoin bills, UK FCA regime, Asian frameworks" is plausible context, but it is not in the update and risks turning a clean regulatory angle into a policy grab bag.
"the end of 'crypto or settlement'" is writerly but mushy. It sounds like a thought-leader deck, not a beat reporter's story.

"Visa, Stripe, PayPal, Mastercard" as comparable moves may be useful later, but here it imports outside evidence the prompt did not supply and could send the founder chasing a broader category story before the basics are confirmed.
